title: Returning After Rebirth to Report
excerpt: (Honghua Monthly, issue 37, July 1944: “News Reported After Rebirth in the West”)

inline.s: (Honghua Monthly, issue 37, July 1944: “News Reported After Rebirth in the West”)

Layman Zhu, personal name Dingyi, courtesy name Jingchen, also known by the courtesy name Xingwu, was a native of Kunming in Yunnan. He practiced medicine as his profession, and in his leisure often cultivated the method of quiet sitting.

, through the guidance of his close friend Layman Wang Jueru, he changed to the practice of the Buddha-recitation Dharma gate and was quite diligent. The following summer he happened to catch a cold and fell ill in bed. Wang Jueru went to visit him and urged him to rest and recover at the renowned Yunqi Monastery on the outskirts of the city, while listening to lectures on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, and accompanied him there. After ten days Zhu Dingyi returned home, and Wang Jueru went to visit him again, finding his illness grave and accompanied by diarrhea. He urged him, saying: “You are a physician and can diagnose and treat yourself. But now that the illness has reached this point, I fear your diagnosis and treatment may not be correct. Why not call in another physician for a consultation, so that you may recover sooner?” Layman Zhu said: “No, no. After you all went to hear the sutra lectures, I had a dream one night in which I saw Amitābha Buddha, and I joyfully made obeisance. Just as I was prostrating with the five limbs to the ground, I saw the Great One in White, his body likewise very tall, coming toward me face to face. As he drew near, fearing that his robe might brush against me, he lifted the hem and floated gently past my side, his smile brimming with warmth. Observing this, it seemed he would soon come to guide me to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, so what need is there to call in another physician?” Not long after, the illness grew still more severe. Knowing his time had come, he entrusted Wang Jueru with inviting a bhikshu to his home to assist in recitation. Thus on the night of the sixth day of the sixth month, he sat in full lotus and passed away reciting the Buddha's name.

When Wang Jueru, on his behalf, invited the bhikshu to come and recite the Buddha's name, Layman Zhu said: “I will certainly be reborn tonight.” Half-believing and half-doubting, Wang Jueru made an agreement with him, saying: “Nowadays, rebirth in the West through Buddha-recitation is attested only by the auspicious signs at death. After one has been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, there is no other conclusive proof. If you attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss this time, you must come back in person to report, proving that you have truly been reborn there. You must remember this well!” Layman Zhu said: “How shall I report?” Wang Jueru said: “Have you not seen it recorded in the books how Que Gongze, reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, came back to report?” Layman Zhu said: “That manner of reporting requires nothing less than the highest grade of the highest birth; how could I manage it? I can only report in a dream.” Wang Jueru said: “That is fine too, so long as it proves you have been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

[Que Gongze] The Biographies of Laymen records: Que Gongze was a man of Hebei. In the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, he lived in Luoyang, living at ease and in delight, free and untrammeled, and every day recited the Zhengfa Hua Sutra. After Que Gongze passed away, his friends held a Dharma assembly for him at the White Horse Monastery in Luoyang. In the evening, during the sutra recitation, a voice was suddenly heard in the air. The assembly looked up and beheld a man whose form and countenance shone with bright beauty, who said: “I am Que Gongze. I have been born in the Western Land of Bliss, and have come with all the good and superior beings to hear the sutra.” All those in the hall saw this vision. There was a man of Ji Commandery named Wei Shidu, a disciple of Que Gongze, whose mother often made offerings of food to the monks. The same day, near noon, a bowl suddenly descended from the air and landed directly before the mother. On close inspection, it was the very bowl Que Gongze had always used, filled to the brim with rice, its fragrance filling the whole hall. Those who ate of the rice in the bowl did not feel hungry for seven days. The eminent Jin-dynasty monk Zhi Daolin praised this deed with boundless admiration. [Zhengfa Hua Sutra] Translated by Dharmarakṣa in the Western Jin dynasty, it is the earliest translation of the Lotus Sutra.

After Layman Zhu passed away seated, in accordance with the Buddha's rule he was placed in the coffin, then cremated, and his ashes were placed in a stupa. When all matters were finished, it was already mid-June. Time flew by swiftly, and in the blink of an eye July, August, and September had all passed, yet there was no news. We even thought that Layman Zhu had not attained rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, or that he had attained rebirth but was unwilling to communicate with us, since the promised report had not come to pass. Unexpectedly, on the last day of the eleventh lunar month, Wang Jueru, suffering from a toothache, lay resting in bed during the day. In a daze, he saw Layman Zhu ascend the stairs and sit down on a stool. (Original note: Because Wang Jueru recited the Buddha's name, his bed was placed beside the Buddha hall upstairs.) His build was as before, and he wore a half-new flat cap and clothes that looked recently washed, all clean, with a radiance shining in. His expression was lively and bright, his face like a full moon, and his skin delicate and tender like that of a handsome boy of eight. Compared with the beard covering his face in life, and his fallen teeth and wrinkled face, he seemed a different person altogether. Had Wang Jueru not been his most intimate friend, exceedingly familiar with him, and a close companion since childhood, he would hardly have recognized him. For such beauty of bearing was something Layman Zhu had never possessed in all his life.

At the sight, Wang Jueru was overjoyed and astonished beyond measure, and in his incoherence he blurted out: “Ah! So you have truly been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss! Otherwise how could you have such a bearing? You yourself do not know that your face is now completely that of a tender, handsome boy. In life you had lost more than half your teeth, and I once invited you to Songzhu Ju to have them set — do you remember?” Layman Zhu said: “Yes, yes. I have come specially to report to you.” Wang Jueru said: “The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands from here, and it is no easy thing to return. Yet you have actually come back.” He answered: “That I have come back here is entirely through the power of faith and vows.” Wang Jueru said: “How did you come back?” He answered: “Very easily — with a single thought one is there; in time you will know it yourself. When one wishes to come back, one looks toward the darkness; when one wishes to return to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one looks toward the brightness. That is all.” Wang Jueru asked again: “Did you see the Buddha?” He answered: “I have not seen him.” Wang Jueru asked: “Why could you not see him?” He answered: “My meritorious practice is too shallow; I have not been born into the pond of seven jewels.” Wang Jueru asked: “If not born into the pond of seven jewels, then where were you born?” Layman Zhu sighed and said: “Alas, the place where I was born is merely the ground of the West. Ah, I suppose it counts as the borderland.”

Before the conversation was finished, Wang Jueru suddenly awoke. Opening his eyes and recalling, he felt that Layman Zhu's words, bearing, radiance, and marks were vivid before his eyes, utterly unlike any inverted dream. He rose and looked at the clock; it was a little past five in the afternoon. A month later, with winter gone and spring returning, Wang Jueru happened to meet Wang Nengzhi, a kinsman by marriage of Layman Zhu. At their first meeting, Wang Nengzhi said hurriedly to Wang Jueru: “How strange! Last winter Zhu Xingwu came several times to talk with me, saying he had been reborn in the borderland of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and had come specially to report. I have long wished to visit you and tell you all this.” Wang Jueru eagerly asked what Layman Zhu had said. Wang Nengzhi related: “The moment I saw him, I asked: where have you been these past few months, and why did you not come back to report sooner? Layman Zhu answered: I was detained in the realm of darkness for a long while on some matter. It was by the grace of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, who sent someone to escort me, that I could take the time to come. He also said: when I was alive, I gave you books on Buddha-recitation — have you actually practiced according to them? You once ran a restaurant and killed many creatures; your offenses are too heavy. From now on, besides striving in Buddha-recitation, you must all the more repent, and you must take up a vegetarian diet and strictly abstain from killing. Rebirth in the West is the portion of every person, and it is very easy; by no means give up on yourself. I deeply regret having taken up Buddha-recitation so late and that my meritorious practice is so poor; you should enter into practice early as the essential thing — and so on.” After Layman Zhu's report, Wang Jueru's friends, hearing of it, all urged him to write it down and publish it, to awaken people's faith. Wang Jueru therefore wrote it out plainly according to the facts, and appended to the manuscript: “I solemnly vow by the precepts that there is not a single false word, and that I have not added or subtracted a single word of Layman Zhu's replies in the dream.” Yesterday he sent the manuscript to this journal by special letter, asking for its publication, and it is now published to inform monastics and laypeople across the land.

Layman Zhu Dingyi, courtesy name Jingchen, also known by the courtesy name Xingwu, was a man of Kunming in Yunnan. He practiced medicine, and in his leisure often cultivated the method of quiet sitting.

, on the advice of his close friend Layman Wang Jueru, he changed to the practice of the Buddha-recitation Dharma gate and was quite diligent. The following summer he happened to catch a cold and lay weary in bed. Wang went to visit him and urged him to go to a famous monastery on the outskirts of the city
(the outskirts)

, the renowned Yunqi Monastery, to rest and recover while listening to the lectures on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, and accompanied him there. Returning after ten days, Wang visited again and found him suffering from diarrhea as well. He urged him, saying: You are a physician and can diagnose and treat yourself, but now that the illness has come to this, I fear your understanding and judgment may be wanting in accuracy; why not summon another physician for a consultation, so that you may recover sooner? The layman said: No, no. After you went to hear the sutra, there was one night when I saw Amitābha Buddha in a dream, and I joyfully made obeisance. Just as I was prostrating with the five limbs to the ground, I saw the Great One in White, his body likewise tall, coming toward me face to face. As he drew near, fearing his robe might brush against me, he lifted the hem with his hand and floated gently past my side, his smile brimming with warmth. Observing his manner, he seemed about to receive me and lead me to the West; what need is there to summon another physician for a further diagnosis? Before long the illness grew worse; knowing his time had come, he entrusted Wang with inviting a bhikshu to his home to assist in recitation, and thus on the night of the sixth day of the sixth month, he passed away seated in lotus, reciting the Buddha's name.
[Lift the hem (kōu yī)] To lift up the hem of the robe.

When Wang, on his behalf, invited the bhikshu to come and recite the Buddha's name, the layman said of himself: I will surely depart tonight. Wang, half-doubting and half-believing, made an agreement with him, saying: At present, rebirth in the West through Buddha-recitation is attested only by the auspicious signs at death; after rebirth in the West there is no other conclusive proof. If you attain rebirth in the West this time, you must come in person to report and prove the truth of it; remember this most earnestly. The layman said: How shall I report? Wang said: Have you not seen the record in the books of Que Gongze's reporting after rebirth in the West? The layman said: That manner of reporting requires nothing less than the highest grade of the highest birth; how could I do it? I can only report through a dream. Wang said: That is fine too, so long as it proves it.

[Que Gongze] The Biographies of Laymen says: “Que Gongze was a man of Zhao. In the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty he lived in Luoyang, aloof, serene, and untrammeled, and every day recited the Zhengfa Hua Sutra. After he passed away, his friends held an assembly for him at the White Horse Monastery, and in the evening they turned the sutra. Suddenly a voice was heard in the air; looking up, they beheld a man whose form and color were bright and beautiful, who said: ‘I am Que Gongze. I have been born in the Western Land of Bliss and have come with all the superior ones to hear the sutra.’ All in the hall saw him together. There was a man of Ji Commandery named Wei Shidu, who had studied under Gongze; his mother often offered food to the monks. That day, near noon, a bowl suddenly descended from the air and landed directly before the mother. On close inspection, it was the very bowl Gongze had always used, filled with rice, its fragrance filling the hall, and those who ate of it were not hungry for seven days.” Zhi Daolin composed a praise for him: “Great is Lord Que, who drank the void and took in spirit; his spirit wrought wonders in the West, his traces answered in the East; he lingers amid the vaults of heaven, his fame resounding, his form resplendent — would he begrudge this single praise, or not reveal himself beyond the dark?” [Superior ones] Men of superior virtue, an honorific for bhikshus, because a bhikshu holds virtue and wisdom within and has surpassing conduct without, standing above other men. [Zhi Daolin] (
) was an eminent monk of the Jin dynasty. His name was Dun, but he was known by his courtesy name. He was a native of Kaifeng. At the age of

he left home, and was friends with Xie An, Wang Xizhi, and others, delighting in the discussion of abstruse principles. He wrote the Treatise on Form-as-Such Roaming in the Mysterious, in which he propagated
form-as-such is empty
, developing the prajñā teaching of the emptiness of nature; he was one of the six great masters of prajñā studies.

After he passed away seated, in accordance with the Buddha's rule he was placed in the coffin and cremated, and his ashes placed in a stupa. When all was done, it was already mid-June. Time flew like a galloping colt; in the blink of an eye July, August, and September had passed, and there was no news at all. I secretly thought that the layman had not attained rebirth in the West, or that, having attained it, he was unwilling to communicate with us, so that the agreement could not be fulfilled. But
(unexpectedly)
on the last day of the eleventh month

(familiar with him)
to the utmost, and moreover a childhood companion of the same village

, he would almost have failed to recognize him. For such beauty of bearing was something the layman had never possessed in all his life.

: “Ah! So you have truly been reborn in the West! Otherwise, how could you have such a bearing? You yourself do not know that your face is now completely that of a tender, handsome boy.
